source.title: C$^{2}$R: Cross-sample Consistency Regularization Mitigates Feature Splitting and Absorption in Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Hao-Ran Jin; Xi-Ting Wang; Shijie Ren; Hong Xie; De-Fu Lian

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates SAE-feature explanations by testing predictions on unseen text, a different measurement aimed at the explanation-generalization issue in V6. It does not measure neuron-pole job shares or report the fraction of individual explanations exceeding a good-score threshold.
record.gate_note: The AutoInterp evaluation uses explanations generated from 15 observed samples and tests activation predictions on 15 unseen samples; scores are averages over sampled SAE latents. These results bear on explanation generalization (V6), but are not neuron-pole counts. Table 7's judge-agreement correlations do not report the share of neurons with good scores. The text's prompts and instructions are examples for the study's evaluators, not instructions addressed to an AI reading or reviewing the paper.
record.test_reason: This is an SAE-method paper (C2R). It uses AutoInterp as an evaluation tool and reports its own method's scores against SAE baselines. The units scored are SAE latents, not a model's own neurons or neuron poles. It does not test whether neuron explanations generalize (V6) or what share of neurons score well (V7). It reports no neuron-pole shares, vision results or neuron-based attribution graphs.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct in substance. The authors conclude that C2R reduces feature splitting, absorption and composition while preserving reconstruction fidelity, AutoInterp interpretability and disentanglement, on par with baselines. They also report that AutoInterp rankings are consistent between GPT-5-mini and GPT-5 (r 0.81–0.94).
record.recipe_differences: Tests SAE latent explanations rather than neuron poles. Explanations are generated from observed activating samples and scored by predicting activations on unseen sequences; this is not the neuron-pole audit method.
record.method_sensitivity: AutoInterp scores vary across SAE architectures and settings; Table 16 reports lower scores for AbsTopK than for its C2R-enhanced version, and Table 15 reports scores across regularization strengths. The study also reports judge-model consistency, but does not provide a per-neuron score distribution.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE-latent explanations written from 15 activating samples predict activation on 15 unseen samples, with mean accuracy about 0.88–0.96 across most SAEs; AbsTopK scores 0.68–0.76. Scores are averages over 128 sampled latents, judged by GPT-5-mini.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Explanations of SAE latents (not neurons), scored by held-out binary activation prediction, achieve high mean accuracy in 2B–8B language models.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning; PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: AutoInterp results are aggregate scores over sampled SAE latents; the paper does not report individual-latent score distributions or the share above a stated good-score threshold. The evaluated units are SAE latents rather than individual neurons. Some reported conditions have no uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: No AutoInterp score rows were left out from Tables 8–16. Table 7's GPT-5-mini/GPT-5 score comparison and Pearson correlations were not entered as rows because they assess judge agreement rather than the share of individual explanations scoring well.

untested.parts: Neuron-pole shares across models, mixture-of-experts models and scale.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron and recursive generalization.
Whether neuron interpretability rises with architecture and tools.
Attribution graphs built from a model's own neurons.
Generalization of neuron explanations from activating examples; only SAE latents are scored.
Share of neurons with good simulation scores, and the effect of stronger explainers; only aggregate SAE-latent scores are reported.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'tests/T2' and its V6 limits_scope label are rejected. SAE latents are a trained replacement basis, not the model's own neurons. All rows are the study's own method compared with others. The AutoInterp prompt calls latents 'neurons', but the scored units are SAE latents. The judge task is binary prediction over 15 unseen samples, and its chance level is not reported.

versions.untested_parts: Qwen3-32B neuron-pole shares and the one-job, two-related-jobs, and not-understood proportions.
Neuron-pole job shares across model sizes, dense or mixture-of-experts models, or trillion-parameter models.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose detection, and recursive generalization.
Neuron interpretability changes due to architecture, regularization, tools, or vision-model estimates.
Attribution graphs built from a large model's own neurons and reconstruction error.

The study tests SAE-latent explanations, not neuron explanations, and reports aggregate accuracy rather than per-latent failures or a direct comparison of explanations based on activating examples with neuron firing across contexts.

The study reports aggregate AutoInterp scores, not the fraction of individual neurons or latents above a stated good-score threshold. It does not compare stronger explainer models; it reports a judge-model comparison.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Held-out prediction scores are generally high but below perfect, and are aggregates rather than per-latent failure rates; this gives limited evidence of imperfect generalization without showing that inspection substantially overstates what is explained (R01–R42).
